texts: mixed: the saying and the sealed obligation on the lanterns are captured correctly, but "the villagers" is a definite plural with a distributive verb, so it owes a per-member rule the parse never emits — no individual villager can be queried as a sayer, even though the parse builds exactly that rule for the lanterns inside the quote. If the body as a whole is what you mean, write "The village says that the lanterns must burn." — a singular collective takes a plain event and owes no distribution; if it matters that each villager says it, write "Every villager says that the lanterns must burn."

bad: the three occasions are bare prepositional adjuncts with no licensed recurrence machinery, so the translator improvised three per-occurrence rules — two of them over-strong (asserting a repetition at every birth and every funeral, which "at births"/"at funerals" does not claim), and the third permanently unfireable, because its premise restricts sessions by a possession link to the Council that nothing in the knowledge base ever asserts. Give each occasion its own finite clause: "Whenever a birth takes place, the Keepers repeat the phrase. Whenever a funeral takes place, the Keepers repeat the phrase. Whenever the Council closes a session, the Keepers repeat the phrase." — that is the shape the instruction set actually legislates, and making the Council the agent of a closing event gives the third rule something real to fire on. ("The Keepers" parsed cleanly here as one named body, but see L2-19 t1, where the same label went the other way.)

bad: three things go wrong at once — "appears in" is dropped entirely and replaced by a static containment atom, so the verb is unrecoverable and a ledger is treated as a place holding the phrase; "the earliest surviving ... ledgers" claims a single unique earliest ledger for what you wrote as a set (a superlative over a plural set has no licensed form at all); and "Watch" is given a proper-name atom that a bare capitalized class word is not entitled to. Write "The earliest surviving ledger of the Watch records the phrase." — a plain transitive verb, a singular superlative (the only kind that encodes), and an of-phrase in place of the "Watch ledgers" premodifier, whose encoding is genuinely undecided.
